result:
I have been thinking lately about the lost art of verticality—not in architecture, but in attention. We live in an era that rewards horizontal scrolling, perpetual motion, the flattening of experience into feeds and notifications. Yet some of the most profound moments I have known happened when I stopped trying to move at all.

Last Tuesday, I sat on a wooden bench behind the library and watched a single leaf descend. It did not rush. It turned in the air like a slow conversation, catching the breeze, adjusting, finally landing in a crack between two paving stones. I did not take a photograph. I did not post anything. I simply witnessed. There is a strange humility in that act, a refusal to colonize every moment with productivity or documentation.

We are taught that idleness is a failure of will, that every unplanned second is a waste. But the mind refuses to be engineered so neatly. In the gaps—the waiting rooms, the commute without a podcast, the afternoon where nothing is scheduled—something older resumes. Thoughts arrange themselves without prompting. Memory surfaces uninvited, like a fish breaking the surface of still water.

I am not advocating for laziness. There is a difference between avoidance and openness. To be open is to allow the world to arrive on its own terms: the smell of rain on hot asphalt, the particular squeak of a bicycle wheel, the way a stranger’s laughter can make you feel less alone in a crowd.

We do not need to monetize our awareness. Sometimes the bravest thing we can do is let the clock run without checking it, let the afternoon dissolve into nothing more important than being present for it. The leaf did not need an audience. It simply fell, and in that falling, it taught me more about patience than any lecture ever could.
